inst.intro: The 130 university, school and department policies for students merge 2,841 statements from 301 universities, and 99 of the 130 apply during the course. The other stages hold few policies, with 4 at the start of the course, 3 during assessment, 8 when misuse is suspected and 2 over time, and none before the course; another 14 give background, 13 of them in the Context stance. By stance, Cross-cutting duties is the largest group with 36 policies, followed by Allowed with conditions with 30 and Only listed uses with 25, and 20 policies give facts and warnings as context. Only 8 policies prohibit AI, 6 encourage it, 3 require something when AI is used, and 2 leave the decision to the instructor or, for theses and research, to the advisor or committee.

stances.prohibit: The 8 prohibitions are stated by 116 universities, and 7 of them apply during the course. The most widespread forbids students to present AI-generated work as their own (P19.04), a rule stated by 94 universities in 132 statements. The others name particular dishonest uses, such as fabricating information or concealing AI use (P36.03, 16 universities), fabricating data, citations or evidence (P74.02, 12 universities) and forging records such as medical excuses (P74.15, 3 universities). One prohibition applies during assessment and treats using AI or unauthorized notes, devices or the internet in an exam as cheating (P22.03, 9 universities), and no prohibition applies at any other stage.
stances.restrict: The 25 Only listed uses policies, stated by 171 universities, limit how students use AI as they work (24 of the 25) and what they may put into AI tools. The 3 most widespread ask students to use AI to support their learning without using it as a shortcut or replacement (P32.03, 71 universities), not to submit AI-generated content without acknowledging or citing it (P36.09, 70 universities) and to keep personal, confidential or sensitive information out of AI tools (P50.06, 59 universities). Others ask students to use university-approved tools signed in with their university account (P92.06, 23 universities) and to keep course materials out of AI tools unless the instructor permits it (P49.04, 18 universities). The only such policy for assessment asks students to check with their instructor before using AI on take-home quizzes, exams or assignments (P22.07, 1 university).
stances.permit: Of the 30 Allowed with conditions policies, stated by 144 universities, 29 apply during the course, and the most widespread make disclosure the condition. Researchers disclose and cite AI in research outputs, theses and proposals (P62.06, 46 universities), and students follow their instructor's requirements for citing AI (P24.08, 27 universities) or cite it in a style such as APA or MLA (P25.07, 24 universities). A second group allows AI as a study aid, for generating practice questions and flashcards (P14.02, 36 universities), as a tutor or role-play partner (P14.04, 12 universities) and for exam preparation (P14.05, 11 universities), while some uses need the instructor's permission, such as summarizing assigned readings (P105.06, 6 universities) and brainstorming (P15.07, 5 universities). When an instructor gives no AI statement, 1 university lets students use AI provided they disclose all use (P06.05), and the only background policy in this stance says that AI use is optional and students may choose not to use or pay for it (P51.22, 8 universities).
stances.encourage: The 6 Encourage policies are stated by 14 universities, and 5 of them apply during the course. Some invite uses beyond assignments, such as planning study schedules (P14.07, 4 universities), preparing for careers (P119.02, 3 universities) and everyday personal tasks (P119.03, 2 universities). Others suggest habits for working with AI tools: breaking complex tasks into parts when prompting (P93.07, 4 universities) and experimenting with different tools to learn their strengths and weaknesses (P93.09, 3 universities). The only policy over time suggests that students consider creating and maintaining an AI portfolio (P134.06, 2 universities).
stances.require: The 3 Require policies are stated by 4 universities, all apply during the course, and all concern documenting or disclosing AI use: 3 universities ask students to document AI use in their intellectual property contributions (P52.07), 1 to disclose AI use in data analysis methods and figure captions (P27.08), and 1 to err on the side of full disclosure when unsure (P10.08).
stances.delegates: The 2 Instructor decides policies are stated by 115 of the 301 universities, and both apply during the course. Students follow the AI rules their instructor sets for each course and assignment (P78.06, 104 universities, 163 statements), and students doing theses or research get advisor or committee approval before using AI in them (P62.03, 13 universities).
stances.none: The 36 Cross-cutting duties policies are stated by 248 universities and include the most widely stated policy in this part. Students are told to ask their instructor when unsure whether AI use is allowed (P10.04, 193 universities, 386 statements) and to follow the university's academic integrity policy, honor code and conduct rules when using AI (P77.11, 56 universities). Of the 36, 28 apply during the course, and several of these concern understanding and checking AI output and writing prompts: students check that sources and citations produced by AI exist and are accurate (P31.04, 30 universities), understand everything they submit (P30.02, 24 universities), refine their prompts through repeated rounds (P93.03, 14 universities) and write clear, specific prompts that give context (P93.05, 10 universities). At the start of the course, 57 universities ask students to read the syllabus and assignment instructions to learn what AI use is allowed (P78.02). Of the 8 policies for when misuse is suspected, 3 are cross-cutting duties; they describe appeals (P64.02, 7 universities) and ask students to report unethical AI use or AI errors (P71.08, 2 universities) and their own inadvertent use of generative AI (P38.01, 1 university).
stances.context: The 20 Context policies, stated by 253 universities, are facts and warnings that ask nothing of students, and they make up 13 of the 14 background policies and 5 of the 8 policies for when misuse is suspected. The most widespread warns that AI output can be inaccurate, biased or fabricated (P31.12, 162 universities, 297 statements); others state that AI rules differ across courses and instructors (P04.13, 120 universities) and that AI use can bypass the practice through which students learn (P41.08, 64 universities). For suspected misuse, 75 universities state that AI violations are handled through existing academic integrity and conduct processes (P36.06), and others name the consequences, from grade penalties (P37.05, 18 universities) to disciplinary action up to expulsion (P37.07, 13 universities), or say that not knowing the rules is no excuse (P10.11, 9 universities). Smaller numbers report that some instructors require logs or reflections on AI use (P26.15, 16 universities) and that AI output can use sources without citation, risking plagiarism (P120.06, 14 universities).

course.intro: The 173 CS course policies merge 1,549 statements from syllabi at 131 universities, and 160 of the 173 apply during the course. No course policy applies before the course or when misuse is suspected, and none gives background; the remaining stages hold 3 policies at the start of the course, 9 during assessment and 1 over time. The stances Prohibit (44 policies), Allowed with conditions (42), Require (41) and Only listed uses (34) are close in size. Cross-cutting duties (9 policies) and Encourage (2) are small, 1 policy states a fact as context, and no course policy falls under Instructor decides.

stances.prohibit: Of the 44 Prohibit policies, stated by 111 universities, 40 apply during the course, and the most widespread ban AI from producing the code students submit. Students may not ask AI for answers, solutions or code for graded assignments (CT17.c03, 50 universities), submit AI-generated code or text as their own (CT17.c02, 38 universities), or use coding assistants and autocomplete such as Copilot (CT20.c02, 25 universities). Some courses ban AI outright, either for any purpose (CT01.c02, 21 universities) or on all graded work (CT01.c01, 23 universities), and smaller groups extend bans to learning uses such as debugging their own code (CT17.c05, 8 universities) and using AI as a tutor (CT08.c07, 3 universities). During assessment, 30 universities forbid AI on exams and quizzes (CT34.c01).
stances.restrict: The 34 Only listed uses policies, stated by 78 universities, allow AI only for uses the course names, and all 34 apply during the course. The most widespread allows AI only when the instructor or assignment explicitly permits it (CT04.c01, 23 universities); others ask students to use AI to support their learning without replacing it (CT40.c08, 14 universities) or their own thinking (CT32.c04, 14 universities), and to use it only as they would a friend or classmate (CT33.c01, 8 universities). A few set limits on code, such as keeping code taken from AI to a few lines (CT18.c03, 4 universities) and avoiding AI interactions that produce solution code (CT19.c03, 3 universities), and 4 universities tell students to assume AI is not allowed when an assignment says nothing about it (CT05.c01).
stances.permit: The most widespread of the 42 Allowed with conditions policies, stated by 83 universities, lets students ask AI to explain course concepts and material (CT08.c01, 39 universities, 69 statements). Other permitted uses support study and the student's own code, such as exam study and practice problems (CT13.c01, 10 universities), review of code students wrote themselves (CT10.c01, 10 universities) and explanations of code, syntax and error messages (CT08.c02, 8 universities); 7 universities allow AI to interpret or explain error messages (CT09.c01). Broader permissions let students use AI on coursework in general (CT02.c04, 15 universities) or as they see fit without asking (CT02.c05, 6 universities). At the start of the course, policies make AI optional (CT47.c01, 5 universities) and say students need not pay for AI tools (CT46.c07, 2 universities), and the 2 policies for assessment let students use AI on past homework after the deadline (CT10.c04, 1 university) or to understand why tests failed after the deadline (CT09.c06, 1 university).
stances.encourage: The 2 Encourage policies are stated by 17 universities, and both apply during the course. Students are encouraged or welcome to use AI tools in the course (CT02.c01, 16 universities), and 1 university encourages them to use coding agents as learning tools (CT21.c05).
stances.require: Of the 41 Require policies, stated by 82 universities, 29 set what students must disclose or record when they use AI. The most widespread asks students to disclose or cite any AI use, permitted use included (CT25.c01, 40 universities), and others name the record, such as the prompts (CT27.c01, 14 universities), the full conversation transcript (CT27.c02, 8 universities) or the exact lines AI generated (CT26.c02, 7 universities). A second group makes students accountable for what they submit; they must be able to explain all code they submit (CT30.c02, 31 universities) and must verify AI output before using it (CT31.c01, 24 universities). A few policies require AI use itself, such as projects built around AI coding agents (CT21.c01, 2 universities) and a paid Claude Pro subscription (CT46.c06, 1 university), and 3 universities ask students to reflect on whether and how AI enhanced or limited their learning (CT28.c01).
stances.none: The 9 Cross-cutting duties policies are stated by 49 universities, and 8 of them apply during the course. The most widespread asks students to check with course staff when unsure whether an AI use or tool is allowed (CT06.c01, 31 universities), and 14 universities ask students to seek help from course staff rather than from AI (CT06.c04). Each of the other policies comes from 5 or fewer universities, for example an invitation to share AI experiences and feedback (OTHER.c17, 5 universities), a reminder to be cautious with AI and understand its limits (CT42.c06, 5 universities), a note that students who used no AI need not submit a form (CT25.c06, 2 universities) and, over time, permission to tell staff when the policy disallows something that should be allowed (CT06.c07, 1 university).
stances.context: The only Context policy asks nothing of students and states that course materials and instructor guidance take precedence over AI output (CT42.c08, 1 university).

inst.intro: The institutional documents yield 249 policies that address instructors, merged from 5,525 statements at 303 universities. Policies cluster early in the course: 96 apply before it and 56 at its start, against 43 during the course, 11 during assessment and 8 over time; another 29 address suspected misuse and 6 give background. Over half of the policies, 145 of 249, take no position on AI and instead set cross-cutting duties, such as including an AI statement in the syllabus. Of the rest, 36 allow AI only for listed uses, 30 encourage it, 21 allow it with conditions, 7 leave the decision to the instructor, 5 give facts and warnings as context, 3 require something when AI is used and 2 prohibit it. The cross-cutting duties are also the most widely stated, at 296 of the 303 universities, followed by the policies that allow AI only for listed uses (167 universities) and those that encourage it (165 universities).

stances.prohibit: The 2 prohibiting policies each come from 1 university. Before the course, 1 university asks instructors in writing-intensive courses to assign writing that students complete without generative AI (P01.02), and during the course, 1 forbids instructors to misrepresent AI-generated content as original work (P74.05).
stances.restrict: The 36 policies that allow AI only for listed uses appear at every stage except Over time, and the most widespread of them concern detection tools. When misuse is suspected, instructors should not treat a detector result as the only evidence of misconduct (P69.02, 63 universities), and 58 universities tell instructors not to run student work through detectors at all (P39.03). Others concern student data and approved tools: during the course, instructors keep student work and identifiable information out of AI tools unless the student consents or the tool is approved (P50.08, 39 universities), and before the course they choose only approved or university-licensed tools (P92.01, 27 universities). At assessment, instructors keep a human accountable for AI-assisted grades (P46.09, 18 universities) or do not use AI to grade at all (P46.03, 17 universities). Before the course, 13 universities also ask them to move exams and major assessments to in-person, supervised formats (P33.04).
stances.permit: The most widespread policies that allow AI with conditions concern instructors' own use of it. Before the course, instructors may use AI to draft and refine syllabi, rubrics, quiz questions and other course materials (P59.01), a policy stated by 50 universities in 114 statements. During the course, instructors may use approved tools to draft feedback or score work against a rubric (P59.05, 16 universities), and 6 universities let them use AI to help draft formative feedback, flag patterns in student responses and generate ideas for feedback (P101.05); when misuse is suspected, they may use detector results only as preliminary or supporting evidence (P69.05, 17 universities). Other policies let instructors allow students to use AI for listed purposes, such as study aids and practice exams (P14.01, 7 universities) or editing and proofreading (P91.01, 6 universities).
stances.encourage: Of the 30 policies that encourage AI, 16 apply during the course, and none applies during assessment. Before the course, instructors are asked to design assignments that build in student AI use (P79.01), stated by 64 universities, more than any other encouraging policy, and to run their own assignments through AI tools to see how AI handles them (P63.04, 37 universities). During the course, instructors teach students how AI works and what it can and cannot do (P44.04, 45 universities), teach them to use it ethically (P44.06, 35 universities), and assign them to critique or verify AI output (P31.08, 28 universities). Only 1 encouraging policy applies over time; it encourages instructors to seek grants and support for AI work (P122.10, 1 university).
stances.require: Instructors may require students to submit their prompts, transcripts, drafts or process reflections (P26.03, 43 universities, 67 statements), and may require them to disclose, cite or explain their AI use (P24.01, 32 universities). The third requiring policy, from 2 universities, has advisory committees attest to the authenticity of a student's work and AI disclosure (P62.21).
stances.delegates: The 7 policies that leave the AI decision to the instructor are stated by 157 universities, and 5 of them apply before the course. Before the course, instructors develop a clear course AI policy (P04.02, 82 universities), which they may adopt or adapt from the provided sample syllabus statements (P110.02, 72 universities), and they may set different AI rules for different assignments in the same course (P04.03, 23 universities). At the start of the course, 8 universities ask instructors to state whether students may upload course materials to AI tools (P49.01). The only such policy for suspected misuse leaves the consequences to the instructor's discretion (P37.08, 16 universities).
stances.none: The 145 cross-cutting policies, stated by 296 universities, set duties for instructors, and 60 of them apply before the course. The most widespread of those concern assessment design: instructors base AI decisions on the course's learning objectives (P83.01, 71 universities), redesign assignments and assessments in response to generative AI (P35.01, 58 universities), and assess students' learning process along with the final product (P35.02, 49 universities). The 42 policies at the start of the course concern telling students the rules. They include the most widespread of all 249 policies, telling students clearly whether and how they may use AI (P09.03, 193 universities, 389 statements), along with including a generative AI statement in the syllabus (P09.02, 191 universities, 323 statements) and explaining how to cite or acknowledge AI use (P24.03, 83 universities); 62 universities also ask instructors to tell students whether and how they use AI themselves (P47.01). The 23 policies for suspected misuse ask instructors to talk with the student in a supportive way before escalating (P57.01, 66 universities) and to report suspected misuse promptly to the academic integrity office (P81.03, 57 universities), and 47 universities say instructors may use detection or plagiarism tools (P40.07). Fewer apply later in the course: 12 during the course, 1 during assessment and 7 over time. The most widespread during the course ask instructors to state AI expectations for each assignment, not only course-wide (P09.09, 85 universities), to review AI output they produce and remain responsible for it (P31.05, 44 universities) and to remind students of the policy throughout the semester (P66.13, 35 universities). The only one during assessment asks instructors to make clear that original, personal student work, not AI-generated content, is what counts for assessment (P29.01, 6 universities).
stances.context: The 5 Context policies, stated by 52 universities, are facts and warnings that ask nothing of instructors, and all of them give background. The most widespread state that AI use cannot be fully prevented and that bans are impractical and hard to enforce (P82.08, 25 universities), and that AI features are often built into tools without clear labeling (P07.08, 23 universities). Each of the other 3 is stated by 7 or fewer universities, such as the limits and ethical concerns of AI grading (P101.10, 7 universities) and the illusion of learning that AI use can create (P43.02, 5 universities).

course.intro: CS course syllabi say little about instructors. Across 19 universities, they yield 13 policies that address instructors, merged from 30 statements, compared with 249 policies from 5,525 statements in the institutional documents. The largest group, 5 of the 13, gives background facts, no other stage has more than 2 policies, and no course policy applies over time. By stance, 5 of the 13 are facts and warnings that give context, 2 leave the decision to the instructor, 2 require something, and 1 each prohibits AI, allows it only for listed uses, encourages it or falls under Cross-cutting duties; none allows AI with conditions. Some are commitments the syllabus makes about the instructor's own conduct, such as never using AI to give students feedback on their assessments.

stances.prohibit: Syllabi at 1 university state that the instructor will never use AI to give students feedback on their assessments (OTHER.c03), the only course policy that applies during assessment.
stances.restrict: At the start of the course, syllabi at 1 university state, in 2 statements, that exceptions to the AI policy are made only for approved circumstances, including accommodations decided case by case (CT47.c04).
stances.encourage: At 1 university, the instructor encourages students to use AI to deepen their understanding and review difficult material (CT08.c04, 2 statements).
stances.require: Syllabi at 2 universities say the instructor discloses when and where they use AI (OTHER.c02), and at 1 university the instructional team may ask students for their AI prompt transcripts (CT27.c08); both apply during the course.
stances.delegates: Both policies that leave the decision to the instructor apply before the course and are stated by 7 universities. Syllabi let individual instructors permit AI or grant exceptions for specific assignments (CT04.c03, 6 universities, 10 statements), and syllabi at 1 university, in 3 statements, let them disallow AI entirely for assignments (CT04.c02).
stances.none: The only cross-cutting policy says that an instructor who suspects AI-generated work may talk with the student about it, file an integrity charge, or both (CT39.c04, 1 university).
stances.context: The 5 Context policies are facts and warnings, each stated by 1 or 2 universities and 8 universities in all. They include that AI can solve nearly any exercise instantly, so submitted code no longer shows understanding (CT35.c07, 2 universities), and that current coding agents can produce complete projects without human help (CT21.c07, 1 university). Others say that future or advanced CS courses will likely have stricter or different AI policies (CT48.c07, 2 universities), that reporting students for cheating is exhausting for the instructor (CT39.c06, 2 universities) and that students flagged for AI use in a previous semester scored lower (CT43.c05, 1 university).

inst.intro: The 97 university, school and department policies for staff and administrators sit most often before the course, where 47 of them ask staff to vet AI tools, write AI policy and fund AI programs. Another 21 apply during the course and 18 over time, 4 apply when misuse is suspected and 1 at the start of the course, and 6 give background, 5 of them facts and warnings. By stance, Cross-cutting duties is the largest group with 59 policies, followed by Only listed uses with 17 and Encourage with 10. Only 6 policies give facts and warnings as context, 3 allow AI with conditions, 2 require something when AI is used, and none prohibits AI or leaves the decision to faculty.

stances.restrict: The 17 Only listed uses policies limit which AI tools staff adopt and which decisions AI may make. Before the course, staff ensure that AI vendor contracts include data protection, privacy and security terms (P65.03, 27 universities) and acquire AI tools only through the university's standard procurement process (P65.05, 18 universities). During the course, staff ensure that AI-assisted decisions are reviewed by qualified people who can override the AI (P73.01, 12 universities), use only approved or licensed AI tools with university data (P92.08, 9 universities) and do not use AI to make final personnel or hiring decisions (P73.07, 5 universities). The one policy over time asks staff to protect ownership of research and course materials and to review the university's guidance regularly (P52.08, 6 universities).
stances.permit: All 3 Allowed with conditions policies apply during the course. Staff and their units may use AI for routine administrative tasks such as drafting emails and summarizing meetings (P76.03, 22 universities) and for institutional functions such as advising and student services, subject to authorization and privacy (P76.09, 8 universities), and they disclose how they use AI in their work (P48.06, 11 universities).
stances.encourage: The 10 Encourage policies ask staff to invest in AI, and 9 of them apply before the course. Three are each stated by 5 universities, and they ask staff to fund AI infrastructure, subscriptions and pilot programs (P122.01), to provide students with no-cost or affordable AI tools (P51.23) and to require students to take AI literacy courses or workshops (P70.03). Others recommend an AI research center (P122.02, 3 universities), new AI certificate programs (P122.04, 2 universities) and a designated referral point where students can reach human help (P72.01, 3 universities). The one policy over time asks staff to promote interdisciplinary AI research (P122.09, 2 universities).
stances.require: Both Require policies apply before the course. Staff evaluate and test AI systems for bias and fairness before deploying them (P98.03, 4 universities) and set up disclosure requirements for AI use (P24.02, 3 universities).
stances.none: The 59 Cross-cutting duties policies give staff the work of governing AI, and 30 of them apply before the course. The most widespread asks staff to review AI tools for security, privacy and compliance before approving them (P65.02, 65 universities), and others ask them to ensure that AI systems comply with laws and university policies (P77.02, 18 universities), to set and communicate AI expectations for faculty and students (P09.01, 17 universities) and to establish standing AI committees (P54.11, 14 universities). Over time, staff regularly reassess deployed AI systems for performance, accuracy and security (P98.06, 18 universities) and track AI's effect on student learning (P55.01, 13 universities). When misuse is suspected, the policies set a standard of proof for misconduct findings (P69.09, 5 universities) and ask staff to provide channels for reporting and redress (P71.06, 5 universities).
stances.context: The 6 Context policies, stated by 52 universities, are facts and warnings that ask nothing of staff, and 5 of them give background. The most widespread reports that the university sets no single AI policy and leaves decisions about AI use to faculty (P04.14, 25 universities), and 18 universities state that their AI policy is required by, aligned with or subordinate to state, system or board regulations (P77.14). Others note that vendor contracts may restrict training on university data and that some AI products retain the data entered into them (P65.14, 8 universities), and that appropriate AI use differs across disciplines, courses and programs (P109.11, 4 universities). The one policy over time notes that safety and surveillance guidelines would benefit from attention to AI-enhanced systems (P76.06, 1 university).

course.intro: Only 1 CS course policy addresses course staff, and it applies during the course. It is stated by a single university. It is a Cross-cutting duties policy, and no course policy for staff prohibits, allows, encourages or requires AI use.

stances.none: One syllabus lets course staff review students' AI session transcripts (CT38.c07, 1 university).

inst.intro: The 167 university, school and department policies addressed to everyone apply mostly during the course (92 policies) or give background (46, 43 of them facts and warnings). The other stages hold few policies, with 10 before the course, 1 during assessment, 9 when misuse is suspected and 9 over time, and none at the start of the course. By stance, Context, the facts and warnings, is the largest group with 48 policies, followed by Cross-cutting duties with 45 and Only listed uses with 43. Thirteen policies prohibit uses of AI, 10 allow AI with conditions, 6 encourage it and 2 require something when AI is used.

stances.prohibit: The 13 prohibitions forbid using AI for harmful, deceptive or infringing ends, and 11 of them apply during the course. The most widespread asks everyone to comply with copyright law and not to use AI to infringe it (P52.11, 48 universities). Others forbid using AI to create malware or phishing (P74.01, 13 universities) or for illegal or fraudulent activity (P74.10, 11 universities), and ask people to avoid using AI to deceive others, including with fraudulent deepfakes (P74.12, 9 universities). One prohibition applies during assessment and bans autonomous AI agents, treating their use to complete assessments as cheating (P07.09, 2 universities), and one background policy says not to list AI tools as authors (P96.03, 10 universities).
stances.restrict: The 43 Only listed uses policies limit what data goes into AI tools, which tools people use and who makes final decisions, and 38 of them apply during the course. The 2 most widespread forbid entering confidential, sensitive or personally identifiable data into AI tools (P50.04, 126 universities) and allow sensitive data only in tools approved for that data type (P50.05, 104 universities). Others ask people to use only university-approved AI tools signed in with a university account (P92.05, 52 universities) and to keep final authority over important decisions that AI only supports (P73.02, 30 universities). Before the course, 63 universities require IT or governance approval before anyone acquires or uses an AI tool that is not already approved (P65.01).
stances.permit: The most widespread of the 10 Allowed with conditions policies asks people to be transparent about their AI use and to disclose or label AI-generated content (P24.06, 90 universities). Researchers may use AI for tasks such as drafting, coding and analysis (P62.07, 16 universities), anyone may use it to create accessible materials such as alt text and captions (P97.07, 8 universities), and people need not disclose AI used for minor, routine tasks like grammar editing (P100.09, 5 universities). Nine of the 10 apply during the course, and the other is a background statement that whether and how AI use is acceptable depends on the specific use (P118.06, 3 universities).
stances.encourage: The 6 Encourage policies concern AI skills, and the most widespread asks people to attend AI training and workshops (P70.11, 15 universities). Others ask people to learn prompt engineering (P93.13, 7 universities) and to structure prompts with a role, task, context and format (P93.06, 5 universities). Three of the 6 apply during the course and 3 over time.
stances.require: The 2 Require policies ask everyone to complete required AI training, often every year or at onboarding (P70.13, 11 universities), and to document AI-derived code sections along with who reviewed them (P27.05, 1 university).
stances.none: The 45 Cross-cutting duties policies, stated by 225 universities, are the second largest group, and 30 of them apply during the course. The most widespread policy for everyone says that existing university policies and laws apply to AI use (P77.09, 145 universities), and the next asks people to critically review AI output for accuracy before relying on it (P31.03, 120 universities). When misuse is suspected, people immediately report suspected data breaches or security incidents involving AI tools to the designated office (P71.03, 19 universities).
stances.context: The 48 Context policies, stated by 248 universities, are facts and warnings that ask nothing of the reader, and they make up 43 of the 46 background policies. The most widespread warn that AI tools may store, reuse or train on what people enter (P50.14, 109 universities), that AI models reflect and can amplify biases from their training data (P53.04, 63 universities), and that entering sensitive data into AI tools can violate FERPA, HIPAA or other privacy rules (P50.16, 51 universities). Others state that AI output may reproduce copyrighted material (P52.09, 46 universities), that overreliance on AI can weaken critical thinking (P41.09, 38 universities), that the university has no single AI policy (P108.02, 28 universities) and that approved disability accommodations are not restricted by AI rules (P51.24, 5 universities). Three apply when misuse is suspected, led by the warning that violations can bring disciplinary action, loss of AI access, termination or legal liability (P37.09, 12 universities), and the one over time says the university supports ongoing campus-wide dialogue about AI (P66.14, 14 universities).

course.intro: Of the 29 CS course policies addressed to everyone, 28 give background and 1 applies at the start of the course. Facts and warnings (Context) account for 26 of the 29. The remaining 3 are spread across Prohibit (1), Only listed uses (1) and Require (1). Most are stated by few universities, and only 5 are stated by more than 5.

stances.prohibit: The one Prohibit policy states that using generative AI for assignments counts as cheating or misconduct under the integrity policy (CT36.c07, 8 universities).
stances.restrict: The one Only listed uses policy treats AI use like help from a collaborator, under the collaboration policy (CT33.c02, 6 universities).
stances.require: In the one Require policy, the instructor discloses their own use of generative AI at the start of the course and expects students to do the same (CT25.c16, 1 university).
stances.context: The 26 Context policies, stated by 49 universities, describe what AI does to learning and what is wrong with its output. The most widespread say that AI output and code can be wrong, hallucinated or misleading (CT42.c01, 14 universities), that relying on AI for homework leaves students unprepared for exams (CT43.c01, 10 universities) and that AI use hinders students' own critical and independent thinking (CT40.c02, 7 universities). Others raise ethical costs, such as AI's energy and water use (CT46.c11, 2 universities), and note that employers assess job candidates without AI (CT44.c02, 5 universities) and that universities acknowledge legitimate uses of AI (CT04.c13, 1 university). Two describe how course rules treat AI: its use is treated like the use of other online resources (CT33.c03, 3 universities), and deviating from the AI heuristics does not automatically count as academic misconduct (CT36.c15, 1 university).
